\chapter{Two at Once}
\label{ch:ar-two-at-once}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two nouns with \ar{و}, offer a choice with \ar{أو}, turn a clause against the one before it with \ar{لكن}, and accept what somebody said with \ar{حسنًا}.}

The pantry and family of chapters 33-36 -- tea, coffee, milk, sugar, salt, meat, cheese, food, a cup, a spoon, a son, a daughter, a neighbour, a friend -- becomes combinable for the first time, joined, offered and turned.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[wa-]{\ar{و} (wa-) — and}

\label{lesson:AR-C38-wa}



\begin{quote}
Chapter one taught the reply to the greeting and said of it: \emph{hear the little wa- at the front; it means and.} That sentence taught nothing. This book has thirty-six chapters of vocabulary and has never joined two words.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{و}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الشاي} \ar{والحليب}} — \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-ḥalīb} — \textbf{the tea and the milk.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الملح} \ar{واللحم}} — \emph{al-milḥ wa-l-laḥm} — \textbf{the salt and the meat.}
\end{quote}

One letter, and it is \textbf{written joined to the word that follows it}, never with a space after it. That is why it looks like part of the next word and why it has been on the page in front of you since chapter one without ever being a word you owned.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{و}} is the same conjunction Hebrew and Aramaic write with a single letter, in the same job, and it has held that job for three thousand years. It is by a wide margin the commonest word in written Arabic: Arabic prose strings clauses with \textbf{\ar{و}} where English would use a full stop, so a page of Arabic has far more \emph{ands} in it than a page of English ever does.

Note that \textbf{\ar{و}} is also the letter \emph{wāw}, the long \emph{ū} inside \textbf{\ar{كوب}} and \textbf{\ar{يوم}}. One shape, two jobs, told apart by whether it stands alone at the head of a word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-ḥalīb}
  \item \emph{al-milḥ wa-l-laḥm}
  \item three at once — \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-ḥalīb wa-s-sukkar}
  \item the greeting reply that carried it all along — \emph{wa-ʿalaykum as-salām}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\ar{و}} written with a space after it? (\textbf{No} — it is joined to the word it introduces.) Which two languages write the same conjunction with the same single letter? (\textbf{Hebrew and Aramaic}.) And where has it been sitting since chapter one? (\textbf{At the front of the greeting reply}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aw]{\ar{أو} (aw) — or}

\label{lesson:AR-C38-aw}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{و}} gives somebody both things. Nothing in this book has ever made anybody choose.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the joiner from the lesson before, and where it is written — \emph{wa-}, joined on
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{أو}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الشاي} \ar{أو} \ar{الحليب}} — \emph{ash-shāy aw al-ḥalīb} — \textbf{the tea or the milk.}
\end{quote}

Unlike \textbf{\ar{و}}, this one stands as its own word with a space on each side. It sits where \textbf{\ar{و}} sits, between the two things, and nothing else in the sentence changes.

Look at the shape: \textbf{\ar{أ}} — the hamza-carrying alif you know from \textbf{\ar{أكل}} — followed by \textbf{\ar{و}}, the letter that on its own means \emph{and}. Arabic's two coordinators are one letter apart and mean opposite things.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أو}} is Semitic \emph{ʾaw}, the same word Hebrew keeps. It is the whole apparatus a host needs: two nouns, \textbf{\ar{أو}} between them, and the question particle a later lesson in this book will add. Until this lesson the corpus could name coffee, tea, milk and sugar and could not offer any one of them against another.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ash-shāy aw al-qahwa}
  \item the same pair joined instead of split — \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-qahwa}
  \item and hear the difference — one hands you both, one makes you pick
  \item \emph{bi-sukkar aw bi-dūn} — with sugar or without
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joiner is written joined to the next word, and which stands apart? (\textbf{\ar{و}} joins on; \textbf{\ar{أو}} stands apart.) Which letter do they share? (\textbf{\ar{و}}.) And which of them makes somebody choose? (\textbf{\ar{أو}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lākin]{\ar{لكن} (lākin) — but}

\label{lesson:AR-C38-lakin}



\begin{quote}
Two joiners so far. One adds, one chooses, and neither of them can disagree with anything.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two items before this one — \emph{wa-}, \emph{aw}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{لكن}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{أسمع} \ar{لكن} \ar{لا} \ar{أكتب}} — \emph{asmaʿ lākin lā aktub} — \textbf{I hear, but I do not write.}
\end{quote}

And with the sentence chapter thirty-seven built, whose verb carries a letter the script ladder has not reached: \emph{asmaʿ lākin lā afham}, \textbf{I hear, but I do not understand}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الشاي} \ar{حلو} \ar{لكن} \ar{الحليب} \ar{لا}} — \emph{ash-shāy ḥulw lākin al-ḥalīb lā} — \textbf{the tea is sweet but the milk is not.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ar{و}} puts two clauses on the same side. \textbf{\ar{لكن}} turns the second one against the first, and it stands at the head of the clause it turns.

\begin{cousinweb}
Look at the first two letters: \textbf{\ar{لا}}, the negator this book taught in chapter five, with an old particle behind it. Arabic's \emph{but} has a \emph{not} inside it.

English did the same thing by a different road. \textbf{But} is Old English \emph{be-ūtan}, \textquotedblleft{}be \textbf{out}, except\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{out} is still visible in it if you look. Two unrelated languages built their adversative out of a word for leaving something aside.

In writing you will also meet \textbf{\ar{لكنّ}} with a shadda, which takes a following noun in the accusative. The plain \textbf{\ar{لكن}} in this lesson joins clauses and asks nothing of what follows.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{asmaʿ lākin lā afham}
  \item the same two clauses with the other joiner — \emph{asmaʿ wa-afham}
  \item and hear what changed — the second clause no longer argues
  \item \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-ḥalīb} … \emph{ash-shāy lākin lā al-ḥalīb}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is hiding at the front of \textbf{\ar{لكن}}? (\textbf{\ar{لا}}, the negator from chapter five.) Which English word was built the same way? (\textbf{But}, from \emph{be-ūtan}, \textquotedblleft{}be out.\textquotedblright{}) And what does \textbf{\ar{لكن}} do that \textbf{\ar{و}} cannot? (\textbf{Turn the second clause against the first}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḥasanan]{\ar{حسنًا} (ḥasanan) — all right}

\label{lesson:AR-C38-hasanan}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{نعم}} and \textbf{\ar{لا}} answer a question. Neither of them says \emph{I am following you}, and a conversation needs that more often than it needs an answer.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the joiner from the lesson before, and the negator inside it — \emph{lākin}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{حسنًا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} — \emph{ḥasanan} — \textbf{all right; fine; very well.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{حسنًا،} \ar{لكن} …} — \emph{ḥasanan, lākin …} — \textbf{all right, but …}
\end{quote}

The ending is one you have written twice already. \textbf{\ar{شكرًا}} and \emph{ʿafwan} wear the same \textbf{\ar{ـًا}}, the two-stroke \emph{tanwīn} over an alif that turns an Arabic adjective into an adverb. The root here is \textbf{\ar{حَسَن}}, \emph{ḥasan}, \textquotedblleft{}good, beautiful.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{ḥasanan} is literally \emph{goodly}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: agreeing, and half-agreeing}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{نعم}} & answers a question \\
\textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} & accepts what was said \\
\textbf{\ar{حسنًا،} \ar{لكن} …} & accepts, and then turns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The third row is the shape almost every real disagreement takes. A learner who can only say \textbf{\ar{نعم}} or \textbf{\ar{لا}} has to accept or refuse whole; this is the first thing in the book that lets them do neither.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ḥasanan}
  \item the three words with the same ending — \emph{shukran, ʿafwan, ḥasanan}
  \item the half-agreement — \emph{ḥasanan, lākin …}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{\ar{ـًا}} ending do to an Arabic adjective? (\textbf{Turns it into an adverb}.) Which two words in this book already wear it? (\textbf{\ar{شكرًا}} and \emph{ʿafwan}.) And what does \textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} do that \textbf{\ar{نعم}} does not? (\textbf{Accepts what was said}, without answering a question.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wa- · aw · lākin]{Two at once}

\label{lesson:AR-R38-two-at-once}



\begin{quote}
Three joiners landed in this chapter. Name them, and say for each one whether it adds, chooses, or turns — and which of the three is written joined to the word after it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-qahwa}, then \emph{ash-shāy aw al-qahwa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the half-agreement — \emph{ḥasanan, lākin …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} five lessons back, the prefix that means \emph{I} — on \emph{aktub}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — every noun in the pantry, two at a time}
This is what the chapter actually bought. Chapters thirty-three to thirty-six taught a pantry and a family that could only ever be named one item at a time — and every one of them is now combinable. Take them two at a time, cold, from memory.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four drinks and their sweetener — \emph{ash-shāy wa-l-qahwa wa-l-ḥalīb wa-s-sukkar}
  \item the same four as a choice, two at a time — \emph{shāy aw qahwa}, \emph{ḥalīb aw sukkar}
  \item what is on the table — \emph{al-milḥ wa-l-laḥm wa-l-jubn}, and over it all \emph{aṭ-ṭaʿām}
  \item what you eat it with — \emph{kūb wa-milʿaqa}
  \item the people — \emph{ibn wa-bint}, \emph{jār wa-ṣadīq}
  \item one of each, turned — \emph{ash-shāy lākin lā al-qahwa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of this chapter's joiners has a negator inside it? (\textbf{\ar{لكن}}.) Which one is a single letter with no space after it? (\textbf{\ar{و}}.) And which word accepts what somebody said without answering a question? (\textbf{\ar{حسنًا}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
